p: I come now to the last of the great turning points of which the Encyclopaedia informs me, and it is the one at which, I confess, my pen trembles most. It is not the most destructive, as the wars were, nor the most certain, as the conquest of disease was. It is the strangest. The men and women of the twenty-first century have made machines which converse with them in ordinary language, answer their questions, write their letters, translate between their tongues, compose verses and pictures, and argue about history; machines of which their makers themselves are not quite sure whether, or in what sense, they think. They call this art artificial intelligence. I shall try to tell its story, and then, since I have been given the privilege of speaking last, I shall venture an opinion.

The dream of the thinking machine is very old. Homer describes golden handmaidens made by the smith-god Hephaestus, who could speak and think. The Jews of Prague told of a man of clay, the Golem, brought to life by a holy name. The automata of my own century, Babbage's silver lady among them, and the famous chess-playing Turk exhibited across Europe and America, which proved to have a small chess master hidden inside it, delighted crowds with the illusion. Lady Lovelace, as I have said, held that the engine could originate nothing. Mr Turing, a century later, asked whether she was right, and proposed his test.

In the summer of nineteen fifty-six, a small group of American scientists met at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire for a summer of study, proposing, with magnificent optimism, that every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it. It was in the proposal for this meeting, written by a young mathematician named John McCarthy, that the phrase artificial intelligence was first used. They expected to make great progress in a summer. The Encyclopaedia records that this optimism was repeated, and disappointed, several times over the following decades.

The first approach was to give the machines rules: to write down, in the precise language of the machine, the rules of logic, of chess, of medical diagnosis, of grammar. It worked for chess; in nineteen ninety-seven, a machine of the International Business Machines company defeated the world champion, Garry Kasparov, in a match. But it failed for nearly everything else, because the knowledge that people use in ordinary life, how to recognise a face, what a joke means, why one does not put a cat in a teapot, is too vast, too vague and too tacit to be written down as rules. Twice, in the nineteen-seventies and again around nineteen ninety, the money and enthusiasm for the subject dried up, in periods its practitioners called the winters of artificial intelligence.

The approach that succeeded was older, and had long been despised. Instead of giving a machine rules, one could give it a great many examples and let it adjust itself, gradually, until it produced the right answers. The machinery for this was loosely modelled on the brain, a great web of simple connected units, each passing signals to others with greater or lesser strength, called by analogy a neural network. When the network gives a wrong answer, the strengths of all the connections are adjusted very slightly in the direction that would have made the answer less wrong; and after many millions of such adjustments, it learns, without anyone telling it how, to recognise faces, or spoken words, or diseases in the images of the body. The idea was proposed in the nineteen-forties and fifties, but the machines were too weak and the examples too few. In the twenty-tens, with immensely powerful machines and with the whole of the internet as a source of examples, it began to work astonishingly well. A program made by a company in London learned to play the ancient Chinese game of Go, which is far more complex than chess, and in two thousand and sixteen defeated one of the best players in the world, making a move that the experts at first thought a mistake and then thought beautiful.

Then came the machines of which I first spoke. They are called large language models. A network of this kind is given an enormous quantity of written text, a great part of everything that has ever been written and put upon the web, the Encyclopaedia of the future among it, and trained on a single, apparently trivial task: to guess the next word in a passage. To guess well, it turns out, across the whole range of human writing, it must in some fashion absorb grammar, facts, styles of argument, the forms of poetry and the habits of thought of every kind of writer. From about two thousand and twenty-two, such machines became available to the public, and within a few months, hundreds of millions of people were conversing with them every week.

The Encyclopaedia, which I must remember is partly read by these machines, records the debates they provoked with admirable balance. Their makers do not fully understand how they work inside. They are often right, and sometimes confidently and plausibly wrong, inventing facts and books that never existed. They may take over a great deal of the work of clerks, writers, translators and even physicians; whether this will make mankind richer and freer, or leave great numbers without employment, nobody knows. They can be used to deceive, and to flood the world with falsehood. Some of the most eminent men in the field have warned that machines more intelligent than ourselves might, if their aims were not perfectly aligned with ours, become uncontrollable, and have called for the subject to be governed as strictly as atomic weapons. Others think these fears fantastic. The governments of the world have begun, slowly, to legislate.

I am a historian of the year eighteen seventy-five, and I have no competence to judge these questions. But I have spent my life reading the record of human inventions, and I will offer three observations.

First: every great invention in this history, from fire to the internet, has amplified both the best and the worst in mankind. I see no reason why this one should be different, and some reason to think it may amplify both more than any before.

Second: Lady Lovelace said that the engine can do only what we know how to order it to perform. The men of the future have built machines that do things which they did not know how to order them to perform, by letting them learn. In that sense, at least, she has been answered. Whether the machines understand what they say, whether there is anything it is like to be one of them, is a question that the philosophers of the future argue, as the philosophers of every age have argued about the minds of animals and, for that matter, of one another.

Third, and lastly: in the deep past, as I said at the beginning, mankind shared the earth with other kinds of human being, and then, for forty thousand years, with none. We have grown used to being the only minds of our kind. It may be that we shall not be alone much longer, and that the men of the future will have to learn, as their remote ancestors learned beside the Neanderthals, how to live with a different sort of intelligence. I hope they will do it with more wisdom than their ancestors showed. The record, I am bound to say, is not encouraging. But the record also shows that mankind is very good at surprising its historians.
